questions.q: Immediately after `h(0)` only (before either CX gate), what are the nonzero amplitudes and on which labels?
options: Amplitude 1.0 on label '000' only
Amplitude 0.7071068 on label '000' and 0.7071068 on label '001'
Amplitude 0.7071068 on label '000' and 0.7071068 on label '111'
Amplitude 0.5 on label '000' and 0.5 on label '100'
questions.explain: The Hadamard acts only on qubit 0, splitting it into superposition while qubits 1 and 2 remain 0, giving amplitude 0.7071068 on '000' and 0.7071068 on '001', with all other labels at exactly 0.

questions.q: After `h(0)` and `cx(0,1)` (control=qubit0, target=qubit1), the '001' branch becomes which label, and why?
options: It becomes '011', because qubit 0 = 1 satisfies the CX control condition, flipping qubit 1 from 0 to 1
It stays '001', because CX only acts on qubit 0
It becomes '010', because the CX gate always flips the control qubit
It becomes '111', because CX flips both qubits 1 and 2 simultaneously
questions.explain: In the '001' branch, qubit 0 = 1, which satisfies cx(0,1)'s control condition, so qubit 1 flips from 0 to 1 — turning the branch into label '011' (q2 q1 q0 = 0,1,1). The '000' branch is untouched since its qubit 0 = 0.

questions.q: After the final gate cx(1,2) (control=qubit1, target=qubit2), the '011' branch becomes the final GHZ term. Which label is it, and what does this illustrate about what CX gates do in this chain?
options: It becomes '101'; each CX gate creates a brand-new independent superposition
It becomes '111'; each CX gate propagates the existing superposition's correlation to one additional qubit, without creating new superposition
It becomes '110'; CX gates in a GHZ chain always flip the control qubit, not the target
It stays '011'; the final CX gate has no effect on this branch
questions.explain: In the '011' branch, qubit 1 = 1, satisfying cx(1,2)'s control condition, so qubit 2 flips to 1, giving '111'. Across the whole circuit, both amplitudes stayed at 0.7071068 the entire time — each CX only propagated the existing split to one more qubit, it never created additional superposition.

questions.q: What is the general recipe for building an n-qubit GHZ state that this circuit is a specific instance of?
options: Apply a Hadamard to every qubit, then measure them all
One Hadamard on the first qubit, followed by a chain of CX gates where each gate's control is the previous qubit in the chain and its target is the next one
Apply CX gates first, then a single Hadamard at the very end
Apply n independent Hadamards, one per qubit, with no CX gates at all
questions.explain: The 3-qubit case used one H on qubit 0 followed by cx(0,1) then cx(1,2); generalizing this pattern to n qubits means one H on the first qubit followed by a chain of n-1 CX gates, each propagating the correlation to the next qubit in sequence.

questions.q: How does this capstone's gate-by-gate amplitude tracking connect to an algorithm like Grover's from Chapter 6?
options: It doesn't connect — Grover's algorithm uses entirely different mathematical machinery unrelated to statevectors

Grover's algorithm is fundamentally the same kind of gate-by-gate amplitude bookkeeping, just a longer and more deliberately engineered sequence designed to grow the correct answer's amplitude while shrinking the others
Grover's algorithm never uses a statevector representation, only shot-based counts
Grover's algorithm only applies to classical bits, not quantum amplitudes
questions.explain: Both the GHZ circuit and Grover's algorithm are, at bottom, sequences of gates moving amplitudes around a statevector — Grover's is simply a longer, more structured sequence engineered so the amplitude of the correct answer grows while the rest shrink, the same kind of bookkeeping traced gate-by-gate in this lesson.
